patch.why: Every test-substitution chain needs a rule saying what analysis evidence is worth. The named base standards revise every 8-10 years (NASA-STD-7009 2008, 2016 and 2024; GSFC-STD-7000 2013 and 2021; ECSS-E-ST-10-03 2012 and 2022, about 19 months from draft to publication), so the next base revision of 7009 falls around 2030-32. The faster route is a NASA handbook, interim or engineering directive, or an ECSS handbook. S2's independent checks (2026-27) and automated statement audits (capability-cheap-trust, 2028 after B-trunk) supply the evidence, so a first directive or handbook naming AI-generated analysis lands around 2029. Verified numerics (2028) strengthen the case but do not gate it: NASA-STD-7009B is already risk-based, and FDA wrote AI-credibility rules without machine-checked numerics. Capped at Medium because it is regulator acceptance. Test-reduction credit written into test standards is modeled in struct-35-test-standards-codify-ai-credit.

patch.status_oct2026: Reliability demonstration by test needs about 230 zero-failure trials for 0.99 reliability at 90% confidence (n = ln(1-C)/ln R); the physical-gate table marks this unchanged unless model-based priors are accepted (then 0.3-0.6x), and no node used that row. Certifiers already trade flights for insight: Space Force certified Vulcan for NSSL in Mar 2025 after two certification flights, and the New Entrant Certification Guide pairs flight-count options with design review (general). NASA-STD-5001B FSR 17 allows probabilistic structural criteria case by case. EO 14335 (Aug 2025) Sec. 3(b)(iii) directs the FAA to review whether to expand the conditions that demonstrate reliability for a reentry vehicle under Part 450 (whitehouse.gov). It concerns public safety on reentry, and mission-assurance certifiers fall outside it.

add_nodes.title: Test standards write in credit for AI analysis
add_nodes.description: A base revision of a structural or environmental test standard (NASA-STD-5001, GSFC-STD-7000 GEVS, SMC-S-016, ECSS-E-ST-10-03 or ECSS-E-ST-32-10) states when credibility-graded, AI-produced analysis may reduce or replace a qualification test, and with what factors and evidence. Credit then no longer needs a program-by-program waiver or tailoring.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: No structural or environmental test standard mentions AI-produced analysis. NASA-STD-5001B (2014) allows no-test options for some metallic structures at higher factors, and GEVS (GSFC-STD-7000B, 2021) allows protoflight and qualification by similarity. Base revisions come every 8-10 years: GEVS 2013 and 2021, ECSS-E-ST-10-03 2012 and 2022, NASA-STD-7009 2008, 2016 and 2024 (physclock-credibility-evidence-standard).
add_nodes.why: Standards codify practice after precedents. Chain (S2): rulebook 2029 -> first structural credit 2030 -> environmental credit on derivatives 2031 -> a base revision that cites those cases 2033. The revision calendar fits only at the optimistic end: ECSS-E-ST-10-03 is due about 2032 and takes about 19 months from draft to publication, so drafting starts while the first precedents land; GEVS is next due about 2029, before them; NASA-STD-5001B will be about 20 years old by 2034. S3 is a year earlier because its precedents are. Codification turns one-off credit into default practice for government buys, where most of the remaining savings sit, since commercial operators already set their own tests. Capped at Medium because a standards body must accept it and no revision is committed to address AI analysis. S2 is Low because about one base revision falls inside its window after its precedents.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Standards follow accidents and experience, and one analysis miss on a flight program would push any revision back a cycle. Tailoring and waivers already deliver most of the credit on risk-tolerant buys, so codification may add little.
add_nodes.signpost: A draft or released NASA-STD-5001, GEVS or ECSS testing or structural-factors standard with a clause on AI-produced or model-based analysis as qualification evidence.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon: codification follows the first credits by two to three years and lands in 2032-33 at the earliest. S2 is Low and S3-S4 Medium. S4 equals S3 because standards revision is institutional.

add_nodes.title: Government missions fly new designs qualified mainly by analysis
add_nodes.description: A NASA Class C or D mission, a Space Development Agency tranche or an ESA mission flies a new-design spacecraft structure or subsystem with no flight heritage whose qualification rests mainly on AI-produced, credibility-graded analysis plus development tests and acceptance-level workmanship screening. The mission-assurance authority formally approves skipping qualification-level environmental tests. This is the government counterpart of physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Government missions use protoflight and qualification by similarity for derivative hardware (GEVS). No government mission has skipped qualification-level tests on a new design on the strength of AI analysis (general). SDA buys satellites from commercial vendors in tranches about two years apart (general).
add_nodes.why: Chain (S2): environmental-test credit on derivatives 2031 -> a risk-tolerant buy extends it to a new design at its test-plan milestone 2032 -> 12-18 month smallsat or derivative build -> flight 2033 at the earliest. SDA tranches and Class D missions move first, because they accept risk and buy from vendors that already qualify this way for commercial customers, hence the hard edge from physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual. Flight dates follow tranche and mission calendars, which are appropriations-bound and equal across S2-S4; S3's lead holds only if a buy reaches its test-plan milestone in 2031. The saving per mission is months and the cost of a qualification campaign, repeated across proliferated buys. Capped at Medium because a government mission-assurance authority must sign. S2 is Low because it chains on a Medium derivative credit with about two years left.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Government programs return to test-heavy practice after any loss, and Class A and B missions will not take this step by 2035. Vendors may simply deliver commercially qualified buses, so the government never formally grants credit and the step is hard to observe.
add_nodes.signpost: An SDA, NASA Class C/D or ESA test plan, approved by the mission-assurance authority, that deletes qualification-level environmental tests on a new-design subsystem and cites AI-produced analysis.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. Dated at the short end of the build lag, about two years after derivative credit. S4 equals S3 because the gate is a mission-assurance signature, which robots do not change.

add_nodes.title: Crewed vehicle structure certified with fewer strength tests
add_nodes.description: A NASA human-rating or crewed-program certification (crew vehicle, lander, pressurized rover or station module) accepts AI-produced, credibility-graded analysis in place of at least one planned static-strength or ultimate-load qualification test of primary structure, at standard factors of safety. It counts when the approved certification plan or baseline deletes the test.
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Crewed primary structure is qualified by test, or without test only at higher factors, under NASA-STD-5001B; NASA human-rating requirements (NPR 8705.2) add independent review (general). Crew Dragon took about six years from its 2014 CCtCap award to certification in 2020 (general).
add_nodes.why: NASA-STD-5001B already lets a Technical Authority approve no-test or probabilistic criteria case by case (FSR 15-17), so a codified standard speeds crewed credit but does not gate it. Human-rating boards add independent review and keep deterministic factors, so the likely first case is small: one strength test replaced on a derivative structure of a station module, lander or crew vehicle. Chain (S3): uncrewed structural credit 2029 -> codified standard and certifiers auditing AI analysis on uncrewed vehicles 2032 (frontier-35-certification-unbinds) -> a crewed program's certification plan, set at critical design review, deletes one strength test 2034. S2 follows its later precedents to 2035. Several crewed structure certifications fall in 2032-35 (commercial station modules, lander cabins), which gives several chances. Low by 2035 in S3-S4 because the most conservative certifier must sign; S2 is Speculative with one year of window.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Crew-safety organizations keep tests by culture and for liability, and one uncrewed failure traced to analysis would end the case. Crewed programs are few and already test flight articles, so the savings are small.
add_nodes.signpost: A NASA crewed-program certification baseline, or a commercial station or lander certification plan, that replaces a structural qualification test with AI-produced analysis at standard factors.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon. It marks the limit of the branch: crewed structural test credit is at most Low by 2035, in S3-S4. S4 equals S3 because human rating is institutional.

add_nodes.title: Qualification campaigns 30% shorter at leading firms
add_nodes.description: At leading space firms, qualification campaigns for spacecraft and launch-vehicle subsystems on programs started in 2031 or later run at least 30% shorter than the pre-2027 environmental qualification baseline of roughly 6-18 months. The cut comes from analysis credit, fewer re-tests, autonomous stands and round-the-clock integration and test. Leading firms set their own test programs, so industry-wide shortening and government credit speed it up but do not gate it. It is the second step after physclock-qual-cycle-compressed (15%, typical programs).
add_nodes.status_oct2026: Environmental test campaigns take 6-18 months. GEVS sets at least 4 thermal-vacuum cycles at spacecraft level and 8 at component level, with plateaus of at least 12 hours (NASA TFAWS 2026, via embodied/research-space.json). Labor (fixtures, instrumentation, axis changes, teardown, troubleshooting) is about 35-45% of campaign time (embodied/s4-embodied.md gate table).
add_nodes.why: The gate table puts environmental qualification at 0.7-0.8x of today in S3 2031, about 0.63-0.72x in S3 2035 and 0.71-0.83x in S2 2035, and at 0.58-0.67x for typical and 0.43-0.50x for leading S4 firms in 2035. Labor is about 45% of a campaign (labor, physics, materials and institutions 45/25/10/20), so robot-run setup, instrumentation and teardown cut it, while thermal-vacuum plateaus and cycles stay fixed. Parallel robot-tended rigs also shorten component reliability trials (0.3-0.5x), which counts here when it shortens a campaign. Robot labor gains alone give about 25% (45% at 2.3x), so the cut also needs a firm that accepts analysis in place of tests; that is the hard edge from physclock-commercial-analysis-first-qual. Programs must start in 2031 or later and report, so the earliest evidence is 2033 in S3 and S4; S2 reaches 30% only at leading firms at the top of its range, about 2035. S4 gets a band and no year. Robots in cleanrooms and test chambers need contamination and ESD qualification on top of process requalification (6-24 months per process), and the first programs on a new robot line absorb that dip. S4 credit meets all four conditions: the gate at the achieving firm is labor and queue, robots do tolerance work at leading firms from 2030-31, no hard prerequisite lands later, and general-purpose robots add to S3's specialized stands.
add_nodes.strongest_case_small: Firms spend saved time on more testing, and workmanship screening and thermal time constants set a floor. Robots on flight hardware need process requalification at each supplier, so early adopters slow down first. Leading firms rarely publish campaign durations.
add_nodes.signpost: A leading firm or GAO reports qualification phases at least 30% shorter than the firm's pre-2027 programs on programs started in 2031 or later, citing robot-run integration and test or analysis credit.
add_nodes.note_2035: New for the 2035 horizon and the branch's clearest S4 effect. A 30% cut sits below even typical S4 programs (33-42% shorter by 2035), so it is High in S4 against Medium in S3, where leading firms sit at the top of a 28-37% typical range and disclosure is the risk. The year stays 2033 in both because the first programs on new robot lines absorb requalification. Thermal-vacuum dwells and cycles are unchanged in every scenario.

patch.thesis: Operators fly hardware qualified mainly by AI analysis about 2029 (base case, Medium). Government credit follows in 2030-31. Test standards and new government designs follow about 2033 but stay Low in the base case. A regulator cap holds 15% shorter qualification at Medium by 2035. S4 robots add a band at leading firms: 30% shorter campaigns, High by 2035 against Medium in S3.
